items.text: In plain words, what does LSAC itself say the Logical Reasoning section tests?

LSAC's own page says it tests your ability to analyze, critically evaluate, and complete arguments drawn from news, ads, scholarly work, and everyday conversation. It lists ten specific skills, not a fixed list of named question types.
How is the current LSAT multiple-choice test structured, section by section?

Four 35 minute sections: two scored Logical Reasoning, one scored Reading Comprehension, and one unscored variable section (either LR or RC) used to field test new questions. Logic Games (Analytical Reasoning) was removed from the scored test in 2024.
What is the LSAT score scale, and is there a penalty for a wrong answer?

The scale runs 120 (lowest) to 180 (highest). There is no deduction for incorrect answers; your raw count of correct answers converts to the scaled score. This track does not claim to raise that actual LSAT score.
Does LSAC itself use names like "necessary assumption" or "strengthen" to label its own Logical Reasoning questions?

No. LSAC's own pages describe ten skills (recognizing argument parts, detecting assumptions, identifying flaws, and so on) and explicitly say you do not need specialized logic vocabulary. The named families used throughout test prep are an unofficial but near-universal industry shorthand for those skills, not LSAC's own labels.
What is a necessary assumption, and which LSAC skill does it drill?
A claim the argument requires to be true, without which it falls apart, but which alone does not prove the conclusion. It drills LSAC's skill of detecting assumptions made by particular arguments.
A GC bids a mold job assuming "this crew can finish in three days." What is the necessary assumption buried in that bid?

Something like "nothing behind this wall will require extra containment time." If that is false, the three day bid fails. But even if it is true, three days still is not guaranteed, so this assumption is necessary, not sufficient.
What is a sufficient assumption, and how is it stronger than a necessary assumption?

A claim that, if added to the premises, makes the conclusion fully and logically guaranteed. A necessary assumption is only the floor the argument needs; a sufficient assumption is strong enough to close the entire logical gap by itself.
What fact would be a sufficient assumption for the claim "this crew can finish the mold job in three days"?
Something like "this crew's documented production rate on identical scopes has never exceeded three days." Add that fact and the three day claim is now airtight, not just plausible.
What is the single most common missed-question mistake between necessary and sufficient assumption questions?

Picking a sufficient-sounding answer on a necessary assumption question, or picking a merely necessary answer on a sufficient assumption question. The test is: does this close the whole gap (sufficient) or just keep the argument from falling apart (necessary)?
What does a strengthen question ask for, and which LSAC skill does it drill?
It asks which new fact, if true, makes the stated conclusion more likely to follow from the premises. It drills LSAC's skill of determining how additional evidence affects an argument.
A trader argues "this team has scored thirty plus points in four straight games, so the over hits tonight." What fact would strengthen that argument?

Something like "three of those four opponents ranked in the bottom five in pass defense, and tonight's opponent ranks twenty ninth." It does not prove the score, it makes the stated pattern more likely to actually predict tonight's game.
What does a weaken question ask for?

Which new fact, if true, most undercuts the link between the stated premises and the conclusion. Like strengthen, it does not disprove the conclusion outright, it just shifts how well the existing premises support it.
Same four-game scoring streak argument from the strengthen card. What fact would weaken it instead?

Something like "the starting quarterback from those four games is now on injured reserve." The stated premise (recent scoring) no longer supports the prediction as strongly once the key player is out.
Can the same fact, reworded, ever answer both a strengthen and a weaken question about the same stimulus?

No, by construction a true strengthener and a true weakener point in opposite directions. But many wrong answer choices on both question types are facts that are true and interesting but irrelevant to the specific logical gap, not actual strengtheners or weakeners at all.
What does a flaw question ask for, and does it care whether the conclusion is actually true?

It asks you to name the specific logical defect in the argument's reasoning. No, it grades the logic only; a conclusion can turn out to be true in the real world and the argument for it can still be badly flawed.
A contractor's pitch says "our last three jobs in your zip code all passed inspection first try, so yours will too." What flaw is this?

It generalizes from a small, self-selected sample of three jobs to guarantee an outcome on a different job with different conditions. This is structurally the unrepresentative sample fallacy dressed up as a sales pitch.
What does an inference, or must-be-true, question ask, and how does it differ in direction from an assumption question?

It asks which answer choice is forced to be true by the stated facts alone, with no outside assumptions needed. An assumption question finds what the argument needs; an inference question finds what the stated facts already guarantee.
A policy states the dwelling limit is three hundred thousand dollars and requires replacement cost be "at least" actual cash value. What must be true, and what would require an extra assumption?

It must be true the payout on a total loss is at least the dwelling's actual cash value. It would require an extra, unstated assumption to conclude the insurer pays exactly three hundred thousand, since that assumes full replacement actually costs that much.
What is the flip side of a must-be-true question, and what does it ask?
A must-be-false question, which flips the logic: four of the five answer choices are things the stated facts force to be false, and the correct answer is merely possible given those facts.
What does a parallel reasoning question ask you to do, and which LSAC skill does it drill?

It strips out the subject matter and asks you to match the argument's abstract logical structure to one of five new arguments on an unrelated topic. It drills LSAC's skill of recognizing similarities and differences between patterns of reasoning, and reasoning by analogy.
"If the Fed cuts rates, bond yields fall. Yields fell today, so the Fed must have cut rates." Which weather argument has the exact same structure?

"If it rains, the field gets muddy. The field is muddy, so it must have rained." Both ignore that something else could cause the observed effect, a sprinkler for mud, other market forces for falling yields.
What is a parallel flaw question, as distinct from a plain parallel reasoning question?

It also matches abstract structure across two unrelated arguments, but the structure being matched is a broken one. The correct answer repeats the exact same logical mistake as the original, not a valid pattern.
What are the two directions a principle question can run?

Find-the-rule: the stimulus gives a specific situation, you pick the general principle that would justify it. Find-the-application: the stimulus gives a general principle, you pick the specific situation that principle covers.

A change-order clause says "any scope change exceeding 10% of contract value requires written client sign-off before work proceeds." Give a find-the-application scenario and a find-the-rule scenario built on that clause.

Find-the-application: which of five job-site scenarios actually triggers the clause (a scope change crossing that 10% line). Find-the-rule: given a contractor who stopped and got signatures before a big scope change, which general policy is that behavior consistent with.
What does a paradox, or resolve-explain, question ask for, and how is it different from strengthen or weaken?

It gives two facts that both seem true but appear to contradict each other, and asks for the one new fact that lets both stand without contradiction. Unlike strengthen or weaken, nothing is being argued for; you are explaining, not persuading.
An adjuster inspects a roof and finds no storm damage. The homeowner's own contractor finds three cracked tabs from the same storm date. What resolving fact lets both be true without anyone lying?
Something like "the adjuster inspected from the ground with binoculars, while the contractor got up on the roof." That explains the gap without either party being dishonest.
What does a main point, or main conclusion, question ask, and what is the classic trap answer?

It asks which answer choice restates the argument's primary conclusion, not a premise, a sub-conclusion, or an opposing view the author rebuts. The trap is a true, strongly worded sentence from the passage that is actually a premise supporting the real main point, not the main point itself.
"Our crew finished the job in record time. We used efficient scheduling. Therefore, we are the best choice for your next job." What is the main conclusion, and what are the premises?
Main conclusion: "we are the best choice for your next job." The premises are the record-time finish and the efficient scheduling, both offered as support, not as the point itself.
What does a method of reasoning question ask for?

It asks you to describe, in the abstract, how the argument is built, for example "by presenting one explanation and ruling out all competing explanations but one," rather than naming a flaw or restating the content.
An estimator argues: "the water intrusion wasn't from the roof, wasn't from the HVAC, wasn't from the windows, so it must be the plumbing." Describe the method of reasoning in the abstract.
The argument reasons by elimination: it rules out every plausible cause but one, and concludes the remaining cause is correct by default, not by direct evidence pointing to the plumbing itself.
What is a point-at-issue question, and which LSAC skill does it drill?

Two speakers talk past each other in a short dialogue; the question asks which statement they explicitly disagree about, or less often, both agree on. It drills LSAC's skill of recognizing misunderstandings or points of disagreement.
A PA and an adjuster both agree the job is multi-trade, but argue over whether a GC was "reasonably likely" needed for overhead and profit. What is the actual point at issue?

Whether a general contractor was reasonably likely needed to coordinate the trades on that specific scope. That single sentence is the disagreement; the multi-trade fact itself is common ground, not the issue.
State the correlation-versus-causation fallacy precisely.

Two things happening together, or one following the other in time, does not by itself establish that one caused the other. A third factor, coincidence, or reverse causation can explain the same data. It is not always wrong to infer causation, only wrong to infer it from correlation alone.
A bettor notices a kicker's field-goal percentage rose every game the team wore their away jersey, and concludes the jersey "causes" better kicking. What is wrong with that?

It ignores the obvious confound: the away games happened to be against weaker defenses. Jersey color and opponent strength are correlated with the outcome at the same time; nothing shows the jersey itself caused anything.
State the circular reasoning fallacy precisely.
The argument's conclusion is just a restatement of one of its own premises, so no actual reasoning connects them. The argument assumes the very thing it is trying to prove.
"This contractor is the best in the area because nobody does better work than they do." Why is this circular?
"Best" and "nobody does better work" are the same claim stated twice in different words. The second half was supposed to be a reason for the first half, but it just repeats it.
State the equivocation fallacy precisely.

A key term shifts meaning partway through the argument, and the conclusion only follows if you don't notice the swap. The argument looks valid only because the same word is being used in two different senses.

A policy excludes "flood." The adjuster uses "flood" to mean any rising water, while an endorsement defines "flood" narrowly as a general surface-water event hitting two or more properties. Where is the equivocation?

The adjuster is sliding between the broad, everyday sense of "flood" and the policy's own narrow definition to deny a plumbing-supply-line loss that fits neither the broad meaning's real intent nor the actual policy definition.
State the composition and division fallacies and the difference between them.

Composition: assuming what is true of each individual part must be true of the whole. Division: assuming what is true of the whole must be true of each individual part. They run in opposite directions.
"This crew finished the job in record time, so every single technician on it is faster than average." Which fallacy is this, and why?
Division. The crew's total speed does not mean each individual member is fast; one technician could have been slow while others covered for him and the team still finished quickly overall.
State the ad hominem fallacy precisely, and what it does NOT mean.

Attacking the person making an argument, instead of the argument's content, as if the attack itself refutes the claim. It does not mean any criticism of a person is a fallacy; pointing out a real conflict of interest is a legitimate, relevant fact. It becomes a fallacy only when that personal fact replaces an actual rebuttal.
"Don't listen to that public adjuster's damage estimate, he's just trying to make a commission." Is this ad hominem, and if so, why?

Yes. It may be true and relevant to motive, but it says nothing about whether the estimate's actual measurements and pricing are correct. Attacking the PA's incentive is not the same as rebutting the estimate's content.
State the false dichotomy fallacy precisely.

Presenting only two options as if they were the only possibilities, when other options actually exist. The persuasive force comes entirely from hiding the other choices, not from any real logical necessity.
"Either you sign today at this price, or the insurance check expires and you get nothing." What other real options does this false dichotomy hide?

Most claims checks do not expire on a sales deadline. The homeowner can also get other contractor bids, take more time, or bring in a public adjuster. The pitch hides those options to force an artificial two-choice decision.
State the unrepresentative, or biased, sampling fallacy precisely.
Drawing a general conclusion from a sample that is too small, or that was not chosen to represent the group being generalized about. The conclusion outruns what the sample can actually support.
A trader backtests a strategy only on five bull-market months and concludes it "works." Why is this an unrepresentative sample?

The sample was never chosen to represent what the strategy does in a down month or sideways market, the conditions where most strategies actually get tested. Five cherry-picked good months cannot support a general "it works" claim.
State the appeal to authority fallacy precisely.

Treating a claim as true solely because an authority figure said it, without regard to whether that person's expertise actually covers the claim, or whether experts broadly agree. A real expert's view is evidence, but it is not proof on its own.
"My insurance agent said this loss isn't covered." Why is leaning on that alone an appeal to authority?

An agent sells policies and is not the one who adjudicates coverage disputes. Their opinion is not the same as the actual policy language or a court's reading of it, and the claim treats the agent's say-so as if it settles the question.
State the slippery slope fallacy precisely.

Arguing that one modest step will inevitably trigger a chain of increasingly extreme consequences, without actually showing each link in that chain is likely. The chain's plausibility is assumed, not demonstrated.

"If you don't let us start mitigation today, the mold will spread through the whole house, then you'll lose the whole structure, then you'll have nowhere to live." What's skipped in this slippery slope?

Whether a short delay today actually makes each worse outcome likely. Each link, spreading mold, structural loss, displacement, is asserted, not shown, and real mold spread rates and structural risk depend on facts the pitch never states.
Why is picking "the converse of the correct necessary assumption" such a common wrong answer?

Because the converse often sounds like it covers the same gap in the argument, but it actually reverses which direction the logical dependency runs, so it is not something the argument actually needs to be true.
How do you tell a flaw question apart from a weaken question when both answer choices describe a problem with the argument?

A flaw question wants a description of the logical defect itself, stated abstractly (for example, "relies on an unrepresentative sample"). A weaken question wants a new fact that would make the conclusion less likely, not a label for what's already wrong with the reasoning.

A trader shorts a stock, it drops, and a friend says "see, every trade you make on a Tuesday wins." Is "pointing out that's only two Tuesday trades" an ad hominem or a legitimate rebuttal of a sampling fallacy?

A legitimate rebuttal of a sampling fallacy. It attacks the argument's actual evidence, the tiny, non-representative sample of Tuesday trades, not the friend's character or motives. Confusing "criticizing the evidence" with "attacking the person" is a common error.
Why does this domain pair LSAC's own named question-type skills with a separate, FORMAL fallacy catalog, instead of treating them as one list?

They answer different questions. The LSAC-derived families (assumption, strengthen, flaw, and so on) describe what a specific test question is asking you to do. The nine fallacies describe recurring, nameable defects in reasoning you will meet in real contracts, claims letters, and pitches, whether or not any test ever asks about them.
